about: Batch 7 (2026-10-25): covers the 9 most-asked (tier-3) topics that had no served question. Seven held-back questions are rewritten around the classic interview question for their topic (DNS, views, DBMS vs file system, quick sort, BST operations, deadlock vs starvation, paging) and two new hand-written questions are added (OSI model, TCP/IP model), plus a new 'process vs thread' question under os.threads (the tier list's os.process_vs_thread was a topic id that does not exist and was removed). Every key point quotes the slides. The OS slides never mention livelock, so the deadlock/starvation/livelock question asks only about deadlock vs starvation. No question is harder than the one it replaces.

cn.dns.hard2.question: What does DNS do, and how is a hostname resolved when the local DNS server does not already have the answer?
cn.dns.hard2.reference_answer: DNS translates human-readable hostnames into IP addresses. A host sends its query to its local DNS server, which acts as a proxy and forwards the query into the DNS hierarchy when the answer is not in its cache: a root server points it to the right top-level-domain (TLD) server, the TLD server points it to the domain's authoritative server, and the authoritative server returns the IP address. The local server then caches the mapping for a while (its TTL), so later queries for the same name are answered without visiting the hierarchy again.

key_points.point: DNS translates hostnames into IP addresses.
key_points.quote: hostname to IP address
key_points.followup: Why do we need DNS at all if computers communicate using IP addresses?
key_points.followup_answer: Because people use names like www.amazon.com; DNS translates the name into the IP address the computer needs.

key_points.point: On a cache miss, the query goes from the root server to the TLD server to the domain's authoritative server, which returns the IP address.
key_points.quote: Client wants IP address for www.amazon.com; 1st approximation: - client queries root server to find .com DNS server - client queries .com DNS server to get amazon.com DNS server - client queries amazon.com DNS server to get IP address for www.amazon.com
key_points.followup: Which DNS server finally gives the IP address for www.amazon.com?
key_points.followup_answer: The authoritative DNS server for amazon.com.

key_points.point: The local DNS server caches the answer, so repeat queries skip the hierarchy until the entry's TTL expires.
key_points.quote: once (any) name server learns mapping, it caches mapping - cache entries timeout (disappear) after some time (TTL)
key_points.followup: If the same name is asked for again a minute later, does the local DNS server contact the root server again?
key_points.followup_answer: No, it answers from its cache until the cached entry's TTL expires.

cn.dns.hard2.quality_note: rewritten (batch 7): classic DNS resolution question; was held back at confidence 0.68

dbms.dbms_vs_file_system.easy1.question: In a file-processing system, the same student's details may be stored in several files. What problems does this cause, and how does a DBMS avoid them?
dbms.dbms_vs_file_system.easy1.reference_answer: Storing the same details in several files is data redundancy: it wastes storage, and when one copy is updated but another is not, the copies disagree, which is data inconsistency. A DBMS stores the information once, in a central database, so a change is made in a single place and every user sees the same data.

key_points.point: Duplicated data wastes storage space.
key_points.quote: Takes up more storage space
key_points.followup: Apart from inconsistency, what is the cost of keeping the same data in many files?
key_points.followup_answer: It takes up more storage space.

key_points.point: If one copy is updated and another is not, the copies become inconsistent.
key_points.quote: May also lead to Data Inconsistency in case of
key_points.followup: What happens if a student's address is changed in one file but not in another?
key_points.followup_answer: The two files now disagree, so the data is inconsistent.

key_points.point: A DBMS stores the data once, centrally, so a change is made in a single place.
key_points.quote: Store information in centralized
key_points.followup: How does storing data centrally help when a student's address changes?
key_points.followup_answer: The address is stored once, so it is changed in a single place and everyone sees the new value.

dbms.dbms_vs_file_system.easy1.quality_note: rewritten (batch 7): was 'name one advantage' graded against two specific ones; now asks about redundancy and inconsistency

dbms.views.medium1.question: What is a view in SQL, how can it improve security, and why are some views not updatable?
dbms.views.medium1.reference_answer: A view is a virtual table: it stores a query, not data, and shows the rows that query returns from the base tables. It improves security because users can be given the view instead of the table, so they see only the columns and rows it selects and the sensitive data is left out. A view is updatable only if each of its rows maps to exactly one row of a single base table; a view built with joins, aggregate functions, GROUP BY or DISTINCT cannot be updated, because the database cannot tell which base-table row a change should go to.

key_points.point: A view is a virtual table that stores a query, not data.
key_points.quote: It doesn’t store actual data by itself but instead stores a query that pulls data from one or more tables (or even other views)
key_points.followup: Does a view keep its own copy of the data?
key_points.followup_answer: No, it stores only the query; the data stays in the base tables.

key_points.point: Views improve security by exposing only selected columns and rows, leaving sensitive data out.
key_points.quote: It increases security by excluding sensitive information from the view.
key_points.followup: How would you let a clerk see employee names but not their salaries?
key_points.followup_answer: Create a view that selects only the name columns and give the clerk access to the view instead of the table.

key_points.point: Views with joins, aggregates or GROUP BY are not updatable because a view row does not map to a single base-table row.
key_points.quote: Does not contain aggregate functions like sum, max, count etc
key_points.followup: Why can't you update a view that shows the total salary per department?
key_points.followup_answer: Each row is an aggregate over many base rows, so the database cannot tell which base-table rows to change.

dbms.views.medium1.quality_note: rewritten (batch 7): adds what a view is; fixed a follow-up answer that confused hiding data with updatability

dsa.quick_sort.hard2.question: How does quicksort's partition step work, and when does quicksort hit its O(n²) worst case?
dsa.quick_sort.hard2.reference_answer: Quicksort picks a pivot and partitions the array so that elements smaller than or equal to the pivot come before it and larger or equal ones after it; the pivot is then in its final sorted position, and the two sides are sorted recursively. When the splits are balanced, quicksort runs in O(n log n) on average. Its worst case is when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, for example the first element of an already sorted array: one side gets n - 1 elements and the other none, so the work adds up to O(n²).

key_points.point: Partition puts elements smaller than or equal to the pivot before it and larger ones after it.
key_points.quote: Rearrange the list so that all the elements in the first S positions are smaller than or equal to the pivot and all the elements in the remaining n-s positions are larger than or equal to the pivot
key_points.followup: After partitioning, where are the elements smaller than the pivot?
key_points.followup_answer: All of them are before the pivot, in the left part of the array.

key_points.point: After partitioning the pivot is in its final position, and both sides are sorted recursively.
key_points.quote: Sort the two subarrays recursively subarray — the pivot is now in its final position
key_points.followup: Does the pivot move again in later recursive calls?
key_points.followup_answer: No, it is already in its final sorted position; only the two subarrays are sorted further.

key_points.point: The worst case O(n²) happens when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element, so one side gets n - 1 elements.
key_points.quote: The worst case occurs when the pivot selection is poor, e.g., always choosing the smallest or largest element. This results in highly unbalanced partitions, where one side has n - 1 elements and the other has 0.
key_points.followup: If the first element is always the pivot, what input gives quicksort its worst case?
key_points.followup_answer: An already sorted array, because the first element is then always the smallest.

dsa.quick_sort.hard2.quality_note: rewritten (batch 7): classic partition + worst-case question; was held back at confidence 0.69

dsa.binary_search_tree_operations.hard2.question: What property defines a binary search tree, how is a key searched in it, and why can a search take O(n) time?
dsa.binary_search_tree_operations.hard2.reference_answer: In a binary search tree, every element in a node's left subtree is less than the node, and every element in its right subtree is greater than or equal to it. To search, compare the key with the current node and go left if it is smaller or right otherwise, so each comparison discards one subtree and the search takes time proportional to the tree's height. The height depends on the order in which elements were inserted: inserting sorted keys makes a chain of height n - 1, so a search can take O(n), while a balanced tree keeps the height near log n.

key_points.point: Left-subtree elements are smaller than the node and right-subtree elements are greater than or equal to it.
key_points.quote: all the elements in the left subtree of a node n are less than the contents of node n
key_points.followup: Where would you find a value larger than the root in a BST?
key_points.followup_answer: In the root's right subtree.

key_points.point: A search compares the key with each node and goes left or right, so it takes time proportional to the tree's height.
key_points.quote: Height of the BST depends on the order of insertion of elements into tree
key_points.followup: When searching for a key smaller than the current node, which way do you go?
key_points.followup_answer: To the left child.

key_points.point: If keys are inserted in sorted order the tree becomes a chain of height n - 1, so search is O(n).
key_points.quote: Tree can attain a height which can be as large as n-1
key_points.followup: What does a BST look like if you insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in that order?
key_points.followup_answer: A chain where every node has only a right child, so it behaves like a linked list.

dsa.binary_search_tree_operations.hard2.quality_note: rewritten (batch 7): two points were halves of one property; now property, search and the degenerate case

os.deadlock_vs_starvation_vs_livelock.ha.question: What is the difference between deadlock and starvation, and how can starvation be prevented?
os.deadlock_vs_starvation_vs_livelock.ha.reference_answer: In a deadlock, two or more processes wait forever for an event that only another of the waiting processes can cause, so none of them can make progress. In starvation, a process is blocked indefinitely while the rest of the system keeps running; for example, under priority scheduling a low-priority process may never get the CPU because higher-priority processes keep arriving. Starvation is prevented with aging: the longer a process waits, the more its priority is increased, until it eventually runs.

key_points.point: In a deadlock, processes wait forever for an event that only another waiting process can cause, so none progress.
key_points.quote: Deadlock – two or more processes are waiting indefinitely for an
key_points.followup: In a deadlock, can any of the waiting processes continue on its own?
key_points.followup_answer: No, each is waiting for another waiting process, so none of them can proceed.

key_points.point: In starvation, one process waits indefinitely while others keep running, e.g. a low-priority process never scheduled.
key_points.quote: Problem ≡ Starvation – low priority processes may never execute
key_points.followup: Under priority scheduling, which processes are at risk of starvation?
key_points.followup_answer: Low-priority processes, because higher-priority ones keep getting the CPU.

key_points.point: Aging prevents starvation by increasing a waiting process's priority over time.
key_points.quote: Solution ≡ Aging – as time progresses increase the priority of the process
key_points.followup: How does aging guarantee that a low-priority process eventually runs?
key_points.followup_answer: Its priority keeps increasing while it waits, so it eventually becomes high enough to be scheduled.

os.deadlock_vs_starvation_vs_livelock.ha.quality_note: rewritten (batch 7): was tied to the bridge example with a speculative livelock answer; the slides never cover livelock

os.paging.hard2.question: What is paging, and how is a logical address translated into a physical address?
os.paging.hard2.reference_answer: Paging divides physical memory into fixed-size blocks called frames and logical memory into blocks of the same size called pages, so a process's pages can sit in any free frames and memory need not be contiguous. This avoids external fragmentation, although internal fragmentation in the last page remains. A logical address is split into a page number and a page offset: the page number indexes the page table, which gives the base address of the frame holding that page, and the offset is added to that base to form the physical address.

key_points.point: Physical memory is split into fixed-size frames and logical memory into pages of the same size.
key_points.quote: Divide physical memory into fixed-sized blocks called frames
key_points.followup: How does the size of a page compare to the size of a frame?
key_points.followup_answer: They are the same size.

key_points.point: A logical address is split into a page number and a page offset.
key_points.quote: The high-order m −n bits of a logical address designate the page number, and the n low-order bits designate the page offset
key_points.followup: Which part of a logical address stays the same in the physical address?
key_points.followup_answer: The page offset.

key_points.point: The page number indexes the page table to get the frame's base address, and the offset is added to it.
key_points.quote: Page number (p) – used as an index into a page table which contains base address of each page in physical memory
key_points.followup: What does the page table store for each page?
key_points.followup_answer: The base address of the frame where that page is stored in physical memory.

key_points.point: Paging avoids external fragmentation because pages can go into any free frames.
key_points.quote: Avoids external fragmentation and need for compaction
key_points.followup: Does paging completely remove fragmentation?
key_points.followup_answer: No, it removes external fragmentation, but internal fragmentation can remain in the last page.

cn.osi_model.easy1.subject: cn
cn.osi_model.easy1.question: What are the seven layers of the OSI model, and what do the network and transport layers do?
cn.osi_model.easy1.reference_answer: From the bottom, the OSI model's seven layers are physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application. The network layer routes packets from the source to the destination across different networks, using IP addresses. The transport layer provides end-to-end communication between applications, with services such as flow control and error recovery.

key_points.point: The seven layers are physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application.
key_points.quote: On the left is the OSI Model, which consists of seven layers: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data link, and Physical.
key_points.followup: Which layer sits directly above the transport layer in the OSI model?
key_points.followup_answer: The session layer.

key_points.point: The network layer routes data across different networks using IP addresses.
key_points.quote: The third layer of the OSI model, responsible for routing data across different networks. It uses IP addresses to identify destinations.
key_points.followup: Which layer decides the route a packet takes through the routers?
key_points.followup_answer: The network layer.

key_points.point: The transport layer provides end-to-end communication between applications, with flow control and error recovery.
key_points.quote: The fourth layer of the OSI model, responsible for end-to-end communication between applications. It provides services such as flow control and error recovery.
key_points.followup: Which OSI layer do TCP and UDP belong to?
key_points.followup_answer: The transport layer.

cn.osi_model.easy1.quality_note: new (batch 7): the topic had no question

cn.tcp_ip_model.easy1.subject: cn
cn.tcp_ip_model.easy1.question: How does the TCP/IP model differ from the OSI model?
cn.tcp_ip_model.easy1.reference_answer: The OSI model has seven layers, while the TCP/IP model used by the Internet has fewer: application, transport, network (internet) and link/physical. TCP/IP has no separate session and presentation layers; their services, such as encryption, compression and session checkpointing, are left to the application layer if an application needs them.

key_points.point: TCP/IP has fewer layers than OSI's seven: application, transport, network and link/physical.
key_points.quote: On the right is the TCP/IP Protocol Suite, which has four layers: Application, Transport, Network, and Physical.
key_points.followup: Which TCP/IP layer does IP belong to?
key_points.followup_answer: The network (internet) layer.

key_points.point: TCP/IP has no separate session and presentation layers.
key_points.quote: Internet stack “missing” these layers!
key_points.followup: Which two OSI layers are missing from the TCP/IP model?
key_points.followup_answer: The session and presentation layers.

key_points.point: Session and presentation services, such as encryption or compression, are handled by the application if needed.
key_points.quote: presentation: allow applications to interpret meaning of data, (e.g., encryption,
key_points.followup: In the Internet stack, who takes care of encryption if an application needs it?
key_points.followup_answer: The application itself, at the application layer.

cn.tcp_ip_model.easy1.quality_note: new (batch 7): the topic had no question

os.threads.easy1.subject: os
os.threads.easy1.question: What is the difference between a process and a thread?
os.threads.easy1.reference_answer: A process is a program in execution, with its own memory and resources. A thread is a unit of execution inside a process: each thread has its own thread ID, program counter, registers and stack, but threads of the same process share its code, data and other resources such as open files. Because of this sharing, creating and switching between threads is much cheaper than creating and switching between processes.

key_points.point: A thread is a unit of execution inside a process, and a process can have several threads.
key_points.quote: A process can have multiple threads running at the same time. This is called multithreading.
key_points.followup: Can one process run several threads at the same time?
key_points.followup_answer: Yes, a process can have multiple threads; this is multithreading.

key_points.point: Each thread has its own program counter, registers and stack.
key_points.quote: It consists of thread ID, Program counter, a register set and stack
key_points.followup: Do two threads of the same process share a stack?
key_points.followup_answer: No, each thread has its own stack, registers and program counter.

key_points.point: Threads of a process share its code, data and resources, while processes do not share memory by default.
key_points.quote: Threads share resources like memory with other threads in the same process.
key_points.followup: If one thread changes a global variable, does another thread of the same process see the change?
key_points.followup_answer: Yes, because threads of the same process share its data.

key_points.point: Creating or switching threads is cheaper than creating or switching processes.
key_points.quote: Process creation is heavy-weight while thread creation is light-weight
key_points.followup: Why is creating a thread faster than creating a process?
key_points.followup_answer: A new thread shares the process's existing memory and resources, so they do not have to be set up again.

os.threads.easy1.quality_note: new (batch 7): 'process vs thread' is one of the most-asked OS questions
